name: Light skin ideal in Japanese culture (bihaku)

lead: Bihaku, literally "beautiful whiteness", is the Japanese ideal of pale, blemish-free skin. A proverb says white skin covers seven flaws, and the preference appears in texts as old as the Heian period.

It shapes a large skincare market: whitening (brightening) products that act on melanin, with ingredients such as arbutin, kojic acid, vitamin C derivatives and tranexamic acid, plus sun protection. Users aim for a lighter, more even-toned complexion.

paras: Routines combine brightening serums or creams, vitamin C derivatives and daily sunscreen or UV avoidance, sold under the bihaku label by Japanese brands. Youth magazines and idols have promoted such products.

Whitening agents vary in safety: general references note hydroquinone, mercury and corticosteroids in some products have documented harms, and lighter skin can be more vulnerable to sun damage. Regulated cosmetic ingredients are approved in Japan.

angle.text: Bihaku routines aim to even tone and lighten skin using cosmetic actives and daily UV protection, so the complexion looks brighter and clearer.

lead: Bihaku (literally "beautiful whiteness") describes the Japanese cultural preference for pale, even skin. The ideal is old: the Pillow Book and The Tale of Genji record it, and the proverb "white covers the seven flaws" holds that fair skin can make a woman look beautiful despite other features.[1]

The term bihaku was coined in the 1990s alongside skin-whitening products, which typically work by suppressing melanin production. Japan's health ministry has approved active ingredients, chiefly arbutin and kojic acid, and vitamin C derivatives and tranexamic acid are also used.[1] Brands such as Shiseido, Shu Uemura and SK-II sell these products in China and elsewhere.[1]

The ideal has been compared to wider East Asian preferences linked to class: pale skin signalled indoor life and wealth, and imitating that look led to products such as face powder and sunscreen, as a forum commenter on T Nation noted.[2][3]
infobox: Arbutin, kojic acid, vitamin C derivatives, tranexamic acid

paras: The preference is documented from the Heian period (794-1185); the proverb "white covers the seven flaws" expresses it. Edo-period women whitened their faces with rice powder, and nobles before the Meiji Restoration used white lead powder, which was linked to lead toxicity in children of samurai mothers.[1][3] In the 1990s the gyaru subculture's ganguro style opposed the ideal and faded by the late 2000s.[1]

Traditional uguisu no fun (nightingale droppings) is now a luxury item; popular products contain sake, rice bran and kojic acid, and several ingredients suppress an enzyme involved in pigment formation.[1] Magazines like Popteen and S Cawaii! promote bihaku products to teens and twentysomethings.[1]

General references list mercury compounds, long-term hydroquinone and corticosteroids as having caused harm in some skin-lightening products, and note lightened skin is more susceptible to sun damage.[3]
